[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "OPERATIVE NOTE
Patient: Donovan, Eleanor  |  MRN: 029-87-4132  |  DOB: 1954-11-03
Date of Procedure: 2025-04-28
Attending Surgeon: M. Kettering, MD
Preoperative Diagnosis: Severe multivessel coronary artery disease; critical left main stenosis; recent non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) 3 days prior; decompensated heart failure with LVEF 25%.
Postoperative Diagnosis: Same.
Procedure: Emergency on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting ×4: LIMA to LAD, SVG to diagonal, SVG to obtuse marginal, SVG to posterior descending artery.
Anesthesia: General endotracheal; intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) placed preinduction.
Findings: Fibrotic, dilated heart with global hypokinesis and moderate mitral regurgitation. Critical 90% distal left main stenosis extending into ostial LAD and LCx. Diffuse calcific disease of RCA and PDA. Ascending aorta heavily calcified. IABP functioning at 1:1 augmentation.
Estimated Blood Loss: 1200 mL; Crystalloid 2.8 L, 3 units pRBCs, 2 units FFP, 1 unit platelets transfused.
Complications: Transient ventricular fibrillation upon aortic cross-clamp removal—defibrillated ×3, reverted to sinus rhythm. Difficulty weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass required 45 minutes of support and high-dose dobutamine/epinephrine. Chest closed on second attempt after 2 hours of open-sternum delayed closure in ICU. Post-repair TEE confirms patent grafts with moderate LV dysfunction.
Procedure Details: After median sternotomy, the pericardium was densely adherent. IABP continued via left femoral artery. A severely calcified ascending aorta precluded aortic cross-clamp in standard location; cannulation achieved via right axillary artery and femoral vein. Cardioplegia delivered antegrade/retrograde. The LAD was a small 1.5 mm vessel with poor distal run-off; LIMA was harvested and anastomosed with 8-0 Prolene. SVG to diagonal and OM2 were placed sequentially. The PDA was bypassed with a reversed SVG from the hood of the previous graft. Total bypass time 168 min, cross-clamp 112 min. Temporary epicardial pacing wires placed. Meticulous hemostasis, two mediastinal drains. Patient transferred to CTICU intubated, on maximum inotropic/vasopressor support, IABP 1:1, open sternum with sterile occlusive dressing. SpO2 93% on FiO2 0.8. Specimens: None. Plan: Continue aggressive hemodynamic monitoring, targeted temperature management, delayed sternal closure in 24–48 hours, low-dose aspirin once mediastinal drainage subsides.
Pathology Intraoperative Consult: Not applicable.
Attestation: I personally performed the critical portions of this procedure and was present throughout."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "NEUROSURGERY OPERATIVE REPORT
Patient: Autry, James K.  |  MRN: 773-21-9845  |  DOB: 1982-12-09
Date: 2025-05-12
Surgeon: S. Nkosi, MD, PhD (Neurosurgery)
Preoperative Diagnosis: Acute right-sided subdural hematoma, midline shift 11 mm, uncal herniation syndrome; polytrauma with open left femoral shaft fracture, splenic laceration.
Postoperative Diagnosis: Acute/subacute right hemispheric subdural hematoma with active bleeding; massive cerebral edema.
Procedure: Emergency right frontotemporoparietal decompressive hemicraniectomy, evacuation of subdural hematoma, duraplasty, placement of intraparenchymal ICP monitor.
Anesthesia: Rapid sequence intubation; total intravenous anesthesia (propofol, remifentanil) with mannitol and hyperventilation pre-intervention.
Findings: Upon turning a large craniotomy flap, the dura was tense, dark blue. Under the dura, 180 mL of acute clotted and liquid blood was evacuated from the right convexity. Active arterial bleeding from a torn middle meningeal artery branch was identified and coagulated. The brain surface was edematous, with obliteration of sulci and petechial contusions over the temporal tip. No frank cortical laceration. After hematoma evacuation, the brain remained bulging beyond the inner table. Intraoperative brain swelling prevented primary dural closure.
Estimated Blood Loss: 800 mL; Crystalloid 4 L, 2 units pRBCs, 2 units FFP, 1 platelet apheresis unit transfused intraop. Mannitol 1 g/kg.
Complications: Transient hypotension (MAP 50 mmHg) during evacuation, corrected with intermittent vasopressors. Brain herniation through craniotomy defect required extended bone removal.
Procedure Detail: Patient arrived intubated from trauma bay with GCS 5 (E1V1M3), left pupil fixed and dilated, CT demonstrated 2.2 cm right SDH, midline shift 11 mm, obliterated basal cisterns. Emergent consent obtained. Head positioned in three-pin fixation, right-sided question-mark incision. Rapid craniotomy with burr holes, bone flap elevated. Dura opened in C-shape. Acute hematoma suctioned, meticulous hemostasis with bipolar cautery and Surgicel. After evacuation and hemostasis, brain swelling was profound; durotomy was extended, and an expansile duraplasty with pericranial graft was performed. A Codman ICP monitor was placed into the right frontal parenchyma. The bone flap was placed in a subcutaneous abdominal pocket for later replacement. Hemovac drain left in subgaleal space. Wound closed in layers. Patient transferred to SICU with ICP 22, CPP 60, on propofol sedation, norepinephrine infusion. Postoperative CT scan pending. Specimen: none. Plan: Maintain ICP <20, CPP >60, hypertonic saline as needed, early repeat CT, consider ventriculostomy if ICP refractory. I was present and supervised the entire procedure."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "OBSTETRICS OPERATIVE NOTE
Patient: Campos, Leticia M.  |  MRN: 884-66-0211  |  DOB: 1995-02-28  |  G3P2002 at 38+5 weeks
Date: 2025-05-14
Surgeon: A. Whelan, DO (Maternal-Fetal Medicine)
Preoperative Diagnosis: Prolonged fetal bradycardia to 60 bpm for 8 minutes, Category III fetal heart tracing, cord prolapse suspected, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, failure to progress at 7 cm.
Postoperative Diagnosis: Same, confirmed cord prolapse with nuchal cord ×2 and true knot.
Procedure: Emergency low-transverse cesarean section under general anesthesia; manual removal of retained placenta; B-Lynch compression suture for uterine atony.
Anesthesia: Emergency rapid sequence induction, general endotracheal with cricoid pressure. No regional due to urgency and maternal hypotension.
Findings: Upon entry, dense meconium noted. The fetus delivered cephalic with tight nuchal cord ×2 and a loose true knot in umbilical cord. Apgar scores 2 at 1 min, 5 at 5 min, 8 at 10 min; required positive pressure ventilation and brief chest compressions in delivery room. Uterus boggy after placental separation; estimated uterine atony unresponsive to oxytocin bolus. B-Lynch suture effective.
Estimated Blood Loss: 1500 mL (quantitative blood loss). Crystalloid 3 L, 2 units pRBCs transfused, 2 units FFP.
Complications: Post-delivery uterine atony leading to hemorrhage, treated as above. Cord blood gas: arterial pH 6.98, base deficit -14, pCO2 64. Neonate transferred to NICU for therapeutic hypothermia. Maternal transient hypotension (80/40) before transfusion responded to phenylephrine.
Procedure Detail: Patient rapidly transferred to OR, left uterine displacement maintained. Midline abdominal entry due to prior vertical skin scar. Low transverse uterine incision performed. A male infant, 3120 g, delivered with nuchal cord reduced. Thick meconium suctioned below the cords by neonatal team. Delayed cord clamping not feasible due to infant condition. Placenta expressed manually, but fragmented; curettage performed for retained membranes. Bimanual massage done. Uterine tone poor; 40 IU oxytocin in 500 mL, methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM, carboprost 250 µg IM, then B-Lynch suture placed with 1-Vicryl. Hemostasis achieved. Uterine incision closed in two layers, bladder flap re-approximated. Fascia closed with looped PDS, skin with staples. Mother extubated in OR, transferred to PACU stable. Neonate intubated in NICU for therapeutic hypothermia. Plan: Monitor for postpartum hemorrhage, serial CBC, continue oxytocin infusion, ensure adequate analgesia. I was present for the entire procedure and performed the critical components."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "SURGICAL ONCOLOGY – THORACIC OPERATIVE REPORT
Patient: Griffiths, Mark E.  |  MRN: 529-14-0377  |  DOB: 1960-07-22
Date: 2025-06-03
Surgeon: L. Okonkwo, MD (Thoracic Surgery)
Preoperative Diagnosis: Locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (squamous cell), Stage IIIA (T4N1M0), with direct invasion of left main pulmonary artery and distal left main bronchus, post neoadjuvant cisplatin/docetaxel x 3 cycles. FEV1 52% predicted, DLCO 46%.
Postoperative Diagnosis: R0 resection of T4N1 squamous cell lung carcinoma involving left upper lobe, left main pulmonary artery, and left main bronchus; single station N1 nodal metastases (levels 10L, 11L).
Procedure: Left intrapericardial pneumonectomy with en bloc resection of involved pulmonary artery segment and left main bronchus stump, complete mediastinal lymph node dissection (stations 4L,5,6,7,10L,11L), bronchial stump coverage with pericardial fat pad.
Anesthesia: General endotracheal with a left-sided double-lumen tube; thoracic epidural placed for postoperative analgesia. Invasive monitoring incl. arterial line, central venous catheter, and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) due to pulmonary artery clamping.
Findings: Extensive fibrotic tumor invading the left pulmonary artery intrapericardially, involving the left main bronchus 0.8 cm from the carina. No macroscopic tumor in the pericardium or left atrium. The aorta and esophagus were free. Level 5 and 6 nodes enlarged but soft, probable reactive. Frozen sections of bronchial margin, pulmonary artery margin, and highest mediastinal node (station 4L) negative for malignancy.
Estimated Blood Loss: 2200 mL; 4 units pRBCs, 4 units FFP, 1 unit platelets, 2 L crystalloid.
Complications: Intraoperative hypotension during PA clamping managed with dobutamine and norepinephrine. Transient atrial fibrillation after pericardial opening, cardioverted pharmacologically. Small air leak from contralateral lung during one-lung ventilation required adjustment of tube position.
Procedure Detail: Posterolateral thoracotomy in 5th intercostal space. Dense pleural adhesions taken down. Pericardium opened longitudinally, revealing tumor invasion of left PA. Intrapericardial dissection freed the PA and PVs. The left main bronchus was separated with careful margin. The lung was removed en bloc with attached PA segment and bronchial cuff. Bronchial stump closed with interrupted 4-0 Prolene, air-tight test negative. Pericardial fat pad flap mobilized and sutured over the bronchial stump. Mediastinal node dissection performed systematically; all nodes removed. Left phrenic nerve identified and preserved. Two 28F chest tubes placed. Hemostasis verified, no pericardial defect closure (open pericardium). Estimated operative time 5 hr 15 min. Patient extubated in OR and transferred to SICU on nasal O2 4 L/min, saturating 94%. Specimens: Left lung, attached PA segment, bronchial cuff, mediastinal nodes labeled by station. Plan: ICU monitoring, aggressive pulmonary toilet, DVT prophylaxis, titration of epidural analgesia, check morning CXR. I performed all critical portions of this high-risk cancer surgery and was present throughout."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "VASCULAR SURGERY OPERATIVE NOTE
Patient: Ostrovsky, Daniel V.  |  MRN: 311-55-8290  |  DOB: 1948-01-14
Date: 2025-06-11
Surgeon: J. Takamoto, MD (Vascular Surgery)
Preoperative Diagnosis: Ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage; hemorrhagic shock (preop SBP 70 mmHg, HR 126, GCS 13).
Postoperative Diagnosis: Ruptured 8.2 cm infrarenal AAA with ongoing retroperitoneal leak; atheromatous debris and free rupture into left retroperitoneum.
Procedure: Emergency open repair of ruptured AAA with a 20 mm Dacron aortobi-iliac graft, left renal artery reimplantation (involved aortic cuff), open abdomen with temporary closure due to visceral edema.
Anesthesia: Emergency RSI with etomidate/succinylcholine, maintained with sevoflurane, fentanyl, and cisatracurium. Intraoperative resuscitation with Massive Transfusion Protocol activated; Level 1 infuser, arterial line, CVC, TEE.
Findings: Upon midline laparotomy, large retroperitoneal hematoma bulging from the left lateral aortic wall, expanding during dissection. Aortic cross-clamp applied infrarenally after suprarenal control preparatory. The aneurysm ruptured anteriorly into the left retroperitoneum at the level of the inferior mesenteric artery. Proximal aortic neck was 2.3 cm, severely calcified. Left renal artery orifice was included in the aneurysmal dilatation and required separate reimplantation. Distal anastomoses to the common iliac arteries bilaterally were friable. Bowel edema and tense abdomen prevented primary fascial closure.
Estimated Blood Loss: 4800 mL; Crystalloid 6 L, 12 units pRBCs, 10 units FFP, 2 apheresis platelet units, 10 units cryoprecipitate transfused; cell saver returned 900 mL.
Complications: Cardiopulmonary arrest (PEA) for 2 minutes after cross-clamp release, responded to one dose of epinephrine and calcium. Acute kidney injury likely; urine output < 30 mL/hr despite mannitol/furosemide. Pulmonary edema requiring increased PEEP.
Procedure Detail: Supine, prepped from nipples to knees. Long midline laparotomy. Immediate control of infrarenal aorta with blunt finger compression. Suprarenal aortic cross-clamp placed for 12 minutes while infrarenal neck dissected. The aneurysm sac was opened, organized thrombus evacuated. The left renal artery originated within the aneurysmal segment; it was detached and reimplanted into the Dacron graft as a Carrel patch with 6-0 Prolene. Bifurcated graft anastomosed proximally with 3-0 Prolene in running fashion; iliac limbs sewn to the common iliac bifurcations. Back-bleeding from IMA and lumbars oversewn. Graft flushed and flow restored first to right leg, then left, with TEE monitoring. Doppler confirmed triphasic signals in both dorsalis pedis arteries. Abdomen irrigated, temporary closure with AB-thera wound VAC applied due to substantial bowel edema and retroperitoneal packing. Patient transferred to SICU intubated, on norepinephrine 12 mcg/min, vasopressin 0.04 U/min, pH 7.21, lactate 8.4. Plan: Continue massive transfusion guided by TEG, keep MAP ≥65, plan for second-look laparotomy and abdominal closure in 24 hours, monitor for compartment syndrome, early CRRT if indicated. I performed the entire emergency procedure."}]

Patient: Juan Dela Cruz

Date of Surgery: 11/03/2025
Preoperative Diagnosis: Acute inferoposterior STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock; failed percutaneous intervention; severe triple-vessel coronary artery disease.
Postoperative Diagnosis: Same, status post emergent coronary artery bypass grafting ×4.
Procedure Performed: Emergent coronary artery bypass grafting ×4 (LIMA to LAD, SVG to OM1, SVG to PDA, SVG to ramus intermedius) on cardiopulmonary bypass; intra-aortic balloon pump insertion via left femoral artery.
Surgeon: Maria Isabella Reyes, MD
Assistant: Luis Santos, RNFA
Anesthesia: General endotracheal with arterial and central venous access; TEE monitoring.
Findings: Dilated, poorly contractile LV; LVEF 20% on intraoperative TEE. Proximal LAD 100% occluded, heavily calcified; circumflex 90% mid stenosis; RCA 95% proximal with thrombus. Moderate-to-severe MR. Calcified ascending aorta. Moderate pulmonary hypertension (PAP 55/30 mmHg).
Estimated Blood Loss: 1200 mL.
Blood Products: 4 units pRBCs, 2 FFP, 1 platelet apheresis.
Complications: Profound hypotension on weaning from CPB requiring high-dose epinephrine, norepinephrine, vasopressin; transient VT needing single defibrillation; IABP placed for hemodynamic support.
Narrative: Patient transferred directly from cath lab after unsuccessful PCI to RCA with ongoing chest pain, on dobutamine, MAP 50s. In OR, standard monitors, prepped and draped. Median sternotomy performed. LIMA harvested pedicled; saphenous vein harvested from left thigh. Pericardium opened revealing tense, discolored heart. Heparin given, ACT >480 sec. Aortic and bicaval cannulation cautiously; CPB initiated, cooled to 32°C. Aortic cross-clamp applied, antegrade cold blood cardioplegia q20 min. Distal anastomoses: SVG to PDA (7-0 Prolene), SVG to OM1, SVG to ramus intermedius sequentially; LIMA-LAD with 8-0 Prolene. Proximal SVGs anastomosed to ascending aorta with side-biting clamp, requiring reposition due to calcium. Cross-clamp removed, heart reperfused. Sinus rhythm returned but LV akinetic. Inotropes escalated; despite that, attempted wean failed with MAP 40 mmHg. A 40 cc IABP inserted via left femoral artery, 1:1 augmentation. With IABP, gradually weaned off CPB. Protamine. Decannulation. Hemostasis achieved with Surgicel and cautery. Sternum closed with wires but due to edema, skin closed, sternum left open with negative pressure dressing. 2 mediastinal chest tubes, 1 left pleural. Patient: Harold Bishop

Procedure: PPPD, portal vein wedge resection/repair, standard lymphadenectomy (stations 8a, 12b, 13, 14, 17), cholecystectomy; retrocolic end-to-side duct-to-mucosa pancreaticojejunostomy with stent, hepaticojejunostomy, duodenojejunostomy.

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "OPERATIVE NOTE: EXCISION OF BENIGN NEVUS
Specialty: Dermatology
Sample Name: Elliptical Excision Nevus Left Shoulder
Pre-Operative Diagnosis: Melanocytic nevus, left shoulder, clinically benign, patient reports mild size increase.
Post-Operative Diagnosis: Same. Specimen sent for histopathology.
Procedure: Elliptical excision of nevus left shoulder, 12 mm x 4 mm, closure in layers.
Surgeon: J. Patel, MD
Anesthesia: Local infiltration, 3 cc 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine.
Findings: A 7 mm x 5 mm, well-circumscribed, uniformly pigmented tan-brown macule with regular borders. No clinical atypia. No satellite lesions. Dermoscopy prior to excision revealed a benign globular pattern without blue-white veil.
Narrative Description of Procedure: The patient was identified and the left shoulder site was verified with the patient. The area was prepped with chlorhexidine and draped in sterile fashion. Local anesthetic was infiltrated to create a wheal; adequate anesthesia was confirmed. Using a #15 blade, an elliptical incision was made oriented along the relaxed skin tension lines, encompassing the lesion with 2 mm clinical margins. The excision was carried through the dermis and into the superficial subcutaneous fat. The specimen was grasped with Adson forceps, elevated using sharp and blunt dissection, and then excised completely and passed off as specimen nevus L shoulder. Hemostasis was achieved with bipolar electrocautery. The deep dermal layer was approximated with inverted interrupted 4-0 Vicryl sutures. The epidermis was closed with running 5-0 Prolene subcuticular suture, followed by skin adhesive strips and a sterile non-adherent dressing. The patient tolerated the procedure well without any immediate complications. Post-procedure instructions included wound care, avoidance of water immersion, and return in 7–10 days for suture removal. Return precautions discussed. The specimen is sent for routine histopathological examination; results will be conveyed to the patient. Estimated blood loss: < 2 mL. Condition on discharge: stable."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "OPERATIVE NOTE: ROUTINE PHACOEMULSIFICATION CATARACT EXTRACTION WITH POSTERIOR CHAMBER INTRAOCULAR LENS IMPLANT, RIGHT EYE
Specialty: Ophthalmology
Sample Name: Cataract Surgery OD
Pre-Operative Diagnosis: Nuclear sclerotic cataract, right eye (H25.1); visually significant, BCVA 20/70 with glare.
Post-Operative Diagnosis: Pseudophakia, posterior chamber IOL, right eye; no intraoperative complication.
Procedure: Phacoemulsification with implantation of posterior chamber intraocular lens (Alcon SN60WF +20.5 D), right eye.
Surgeon: M. Okonkwo, MD, PhD
Anesthesia: Topical proparacaine 0.5% and intracameral 1% preservative-free lidocaine; monitored anesthesia care by anesthesia team.
Findings: Clear cornea, deep anterior chamber, 3+ nuclear sclerosis, normal iris architecture, no pseudoexfoliation, intact zonules. Normal vitreous base. Macula flat on funduscopic exam.
Narrative Description of Procedure: After informed consent was re-verified, the patient was positioned supine and the right eye prepped with 5% povidone-iodine to lids and lashes, then draped in standard ophthalmic sterile fashion. A wire lid speculum was inserted. A clear corneal temporal two-plane incision was made with a 2.2 mm keratome; the anterior chamber was entered under viscoelastic (sodium hyaluronate 1.4%). A paracentesis was made superonasally for bimanual instrumentation. A continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis approximately 5.5 mm was completed with Utrata forceps. Hydrodissection and hydrodelineation were performed using balanced salt solution (BSS), mobilizing the nucleus without zonular stress. Phacoemulsification was performed using a divide-and-conquer technique with the Centurion Vision System, utilizing a 45-degree angled phaco tip with torsional ultrasound. Total phaco time 8.2 seconds, cumulative dissipated energy 5.4. Residual cortical material was removed via irrigation/aspiration handpiece. The capsular bag was inflated with viscoelastic, and the foldable acrylic posterior chamber IOL (Alcon SN60WF +20.5 D) was injected into the capsular bag using a Monarch III D cartridge. The IOL was rotated to a centered position and the haptics confirmed in the bag. Viscoelastic was thoroughly removed from the anterior chamber and behind the optic via irrigation/aspiration. The wound was tested to be watertight with BSS; one stromal hydration was performed. Intracameral moxifloxacin 0.5% (0.1 mL) was instilled. A collagen shield soaked in dexamethasone/phenylephrine was placed under the lower lid. The lid speculum was removed, and the eye patched with a protective shield. The patient tolerated the procedure well, remained hemodynamically stable, and no vitreous loss, hyphema, or capsule tear was observed. Postoperative instructions included levofloxacin and prednisolone acetate 1% drops four times daily, avoidance of heavy lifting and eye rubbing, and follow-up in clinic the next day. BCVA checked at day 1 post-op visit expected."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "OPERATIVE NOTE: SIMPLE EXTRACTION OF TOOTH #30 (MANDIBULAR RIGHT FIRST MOLAR)
Specialty: Dentistry / Oral Surgery
Sample Name: Non-surgical extraction #30
Pre-Operative Diagnosis: Non-restorable caries, tooth #30 with necrotic pulp and loss of buccal wall; periapical radiolucency visible on periapical radiograph.
Post-Operative Diagnosis: Same; uncomplicated extraction socket.
Procedure: Simple forceps extraction of tooth #30 under local anesthesia.
Operator: D. Calloway, DDS
Anesthesia: Inferior alveolar nerve block, long buccal, and lingual infiltration: 3.6 mL 2% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine.
Findings: Grossly decayed mandibular right first molar with complete crown destruction, remaining root fragments; no mobility pre-extraction. Periodontal ligament space intact. No adjacent tooth pathology.
Narrative Description of Procedure: Informed consent was obtained and reviewed. The patient was positioned supinely. The right mandibular quadrant was anesthetized via IAN block (1.8 mL), long buccal (0.9 mL), and lingual (0.9 mL) using a 27-gauge long needle; lip and tongue paresthesia confirmed adequacy. A 2.5-min latency was observed. A #9 Molt periosteal elevator was used to reflect the gingival margin circumferentially around #30. The extraction was accomplished using an English pattern forceps (#150), applying steady apical pressure and rotational motion to sever the periodontal ligament fibers. The tooth was delivered in two fragments (mesial root and distal root) without excessive force; both root apices intact on inspection. Granulation tissue was gently curetted from the socket with a Lucas surgical curette. The socket was thoroughly irrigated with sterile saline. Hemostasis was achieved with direct pressure using a moist gauze pack for 5 minutes; no active bleeding remained. A gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) was placed into the socket for clot stabilization. Post-operative instructions were given verbally and in writing: maintain gauze pressure for 30 min, avoid spitting, use of straws, smoking, or vigorous rinsing for 48 hours, soft diet, analgesia with ibuprofen 400 mg p.r.n., and ice pack application for swelling. The patient was asked to return if any significant bleeding, persistent numbness beyond 6 hours, or signs of infection occur. The patient remained alert and was discharged in good condition. Estimated blood loss < 2 mL. No suture required. Follow-up not routinely needed unless complications arise."}]

[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an LLM as part of a medical assistant system, interacting with medical practitioners to improve efficiency."}, {"role": "user", "content": "PROCEDURE NOTE: SCREENING COLONOSCOPY IN AN AVERAGE-RISK ADULT
Specialty: Gastroenterology
Sample Name: Diagnostic Colonoscopy, Screening

Hypopharynx: pyriform sinuses clear, post-cricoid region unremarkable, no masses or ulcerations. Procedure: The patient arrived having performed a single Fleet enema 2 hours prior, as instructed. She was placed in the left lateral decubitus position with hips and knees flexed. A high-resolution anorectal manometry catheter with 12 circumferential sensing points and a distal inflatable balloon (Medtronic ManoScan 360) was calibrated at room temperature and zeroed to atmospheric pressure. The catheter was lubricated and gently inserted into the rectum to a depth of 10 cm. A 5-minute accommodation period was allowed. Baseline resting anal pressure was measured over 30 seconds of quiet respiration. Squeeze pressure was assessed by asking the patient to maximally contract the anal sphincter for 5 seconds, repeated three times with 30-second rests. For simulated defecation, the patient was asked to “bear down as if having a bowel movement”; this was repeated three times. Rectal sensation thresholds were evaluated by inflating the balloon in 10 mL increments: first constant sensation was noted at 40 mL, urge to defecate at 85 mL, and maximum tolerable volume at 170 mL. The rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) was assessed with rapid balloon inflation at volumes 10–50 mL; RAIR was present at 30 mL. The balloon expulsion test was performed using a 50 mL water-filled balloon placed in the rectum; the patient was seated on a commode and given 2 minutes to expel the balloon. She was unable to expel it, indicating a functional obstruction. No adverse events occurred; the patient experienced mild discomfort during balloon inflation but no pain.

During simulated defecation, anal pressures paradoxically increased rather than decreased (mean increase +22 mmHg), consistent with dyssynergic defecation (type I). The balloon expulsion test was failed. Rectal sensation thresholds were within normal limits. RAIR was present, ruling out Hirschsprung’s disease. The rectal pressure pattern showed sufficient propulsive force (mean intrarectal pressure 62 mmHg, normal >45 mmHg). Impression: Functional defecation disorder, predominantly dyssynergic defecation with inadequate relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles and mild anal hypertonia. Biofeedback therapy is recommended.
Narrative: This 51-year-old female has refractory constipation unresponsive to fiber and osmotic laxatives. No pelvic surgeries.
